## Common Collocations
- **celebrar una reunión** — to hold a meeting; **celebrar**, not **tener** in formal register (though **tener** is common informally)
- **tomar una decisión** — to make a decision; **tomar**, not **hacer** in formal register
- **presentar un informe** — to submit/present a report
- **cumplir con el plazo** — to meet the deadline; **cumplir con**, not just **cumplir**
- **cerrar un trato** — to close a deal
- **rendir cuentas** — to be accountable / to report; literally "to render accounts"
- **dar de alta / dar de baja** — to register / to deregister; common in HR and bureaucracy
- **poner al tanto** — to bring up to speed; **Ponme al tanto** = Bring me up to speed

## False Cognates and Tricky Translations
- **la factura** vs **factory**: **Factura** means invoice/bill. A factory is **una fábrica**. Very common mistake.
- **la competencia** vs **competence/competition**: Both meanings in one word. **La competencia es fuerte** = The competition is strong. **Tiene mucha competencia** = He/she has a lot of competence. Context is the only guide.
- **el éxito** vs **exit**: **Éxito** means success. An exit is **una salida**. Classic false cognate.
- **atender** vs **attend**: **Atender** means to serve, assist, or pay attention to. To attend (be present at) = **asistir a**. Both are high-frequency false cognates.
- **realizar** vs **realize**: **Realizar** means to carry out or accomplish. To realize (become aware) = **darse cuenta de**. Already noted in philosophy cluster — reinforce here.
- **el resumen** vs **resume**: **Resumen** means summary. A resume/CV is **un currículum (vitae)** or **una hoja de vida** (Colombia).

## Dialect Variations
- **la reunión** vs **la junta**: Mexico and Central America strongly prefer **junta** for meetings. Spain and South America use **reunión**. Both are understood everywhere.
- **el computador** vs **el ordenador** vs **la computadora**: Computer terminology varies. Spain: **ordenador**. Mexico/Central America: **computadora** (feminine). Colombia/some South America: **computador** (masculine).
- **email**: **El correo electrónico** (formal/universal), **el email** or **el mail** (informal, widespread), **el correo** (shorthand).
- **estimado/a** universality: Standard across all regions for formal correspondence. No significant variation.
- **capacitar** vs **formar**: Spain uses **formar** for professional training. Latin America uses **capacitar**. Both are understood everywhere.

## Cultural and Pragmatic Notes
- **Formality gradient in business**: Spanish business communication is more formal than English. First emails use **usted** and **estimado/a**. Switching to **tú** happens only when the other person explicitly invites it or uses it first. When in doubt, use **usted**.
- **The colon after greetings**: Spanish formal letters use a colon (**Estimado Sr. López:**), not a comma. This is a small detail that signals competence in written register.
- **Bureaucratic Spanish**: Dealing with government offices, banks, and institutions requires a specific register. **Tramitar**, **dar de alta**, **por medio de la presente** are essential. This register is more formal than business Spanish and can be opaque even to native speakers.
- **Meeting culture**: Meetings in many Latin American countries start later than the scheduled time. Arriving exactly on time is fine, but arriving early and expecting others to be punctual may cause frustration. This varies significantly by country and company culture.
- **Register shifting (D-05)**: Professional vocabulary demands consistent **usted** forms, formal closings, and connector usage. Accidentally dropping into **tú** in a formal email is a serious register error. This cluster is where D-05 register shifting meets real-world application.

## Pronunciation Alerts
- **reunión** — stress on final syllable: re-u-NIÓN. Three syllables — the **eu** is NOT a diphthong (hiatus). Written accent required.
- **presupuesto** — four syllables: pre-su-PUES-to. The **ue** is a diphthong (one syllable).
- **acta** — two syllables: AC-ta. Feminine but uses **el** — **el acta**, **las actas**.
- **objetivo** — four syllables: ob-je-TI-vo. Not ob-JE-ti-vo.
- **éxito** — stress on first syllable: É-xi-to. Written accent required (esdrújula). English speakers stress the second syllable.
